question: Which statement best describes React.memo?
options: useMemo caches the result of an expensive computation and only recomputes it when one of its dependencies changes. It is useful both for avoiding costly recalculations (sorting/filtering large arrays) and for keeping object/array references stable so memoized children can bail out. The common mistake is memoizing trivial computations, where the cost of dependency comparison and storage outweighs simply recomputing the value.

React.memo is a higher-order component that wraps a function component and skips re-rendering it when its props are shallowly equal to the previous render. It matters because, by default, a child re-renders whenever its parent does even if nothing the child cares about changed. The key gotcha is that the bail-out only fires when every prop is referentially equal, so passing inline objects or arrow functions defeats it entirely.

Referential equality means two non-primitive values are 'the same' only when they point to the identical instance in memory, not when they merely look alike. React relies on it for both React.memo prop checks and hook dependency arrays, because deep comparison every render would be too expensive. Nearly every 'my memo doesn't work' or 'my effect runs every render' bug traces back to a new object/array/function reference being created inline each render.

useCallback returns a memoized function reference that stays stable across renders until its dependencies change; it is exactly equivalent to useMemo(() => fn, deps). Its primary purpose is to keep handler props stable so React.memo children actually skip re-rendering and so effects don't re-run unnecessarily. It is pointless when the function isn't passed to a memoized child or used as a dependency, where it only adds overhead.

React.memo's default comparison is shallow: it compares each prop one level deep using Object.is — primitives by value, objects and functions by reference. It does NOT recurse into nested objects, so a prop whose top-level reference is unchanged is treated as equal even if a deeply nested field mutated. This is why mutating an object in place (rather than creating a new one) can cause memo to wrongly skip a needed render.

React.memo accepts an optional second argument, areEqual(prevProps, nextProps), letting you control exactly when to re-render — returning true skips the render. It is handy when shallow comparison is insufficient and you want to compare only specific fields or do a controlled deep check. The gotcha is that a heavy comparator can cost more than the re-render it avoids, and it's easy to introduce bugs by forgetting a prop that should trigger an update.

Unstable props are object, array, or function values created fresh on every render (inline literals like {} , [] , or () => {}), giving them a new reference each time. Passed to a memoized child, they guarantee the shallow comparison fails so the child re-renders anyway, turning React.memo into pure overhead. The fix is to stabilize them with useMemo/useCallback or hoist truly constant values outside the component.

Memoization is not free: React must store the previous value and run a comparison on every render, so for cheap components or computations the comparison can cost as much as the work it skips. Blanket-wrapping every component in React.memo or every value in useMemo often makes an app slightly slower and harder to read. Profile first with the React DevTools Profiler, then memoize only where the skipped work is meaningful and the props can be kept stable.
